outcomes: Students will complete a course-appropriate writing assignment that demonstrates mastery of the six elements of effective writing: 1) unity/focus through a controlling thesis claim 2) development/support/elaboration 3) coherence/organization 4) style 5) conventions of Standard Written English 6) conventions of manuscript format.

objectives: Common Course Numbering Language: Critically read, analyze, compare, and evaluate diverse complex literary texts.
Common Course Numbering Language: Reflect critically on one’s own thought processes to identify and avoid cognitive biases and common fallacies of language and thought.

Common Course Numbering Language: Compose thesis-driven arguments to suit a variety of rhetorical situations, including interpretation, evaluation, and literary analysis, supporting them with a variety of appropriate textual evidence and examples.
Common Course Numbering Language: Identify a text's premise(s) and/or assumptions in various social, historical, cultural, psychological, or aesthetic contexts.

Common Course Numbering Language: Analyze and employ logical and structural methods such as inductive and deductive reasoning, causation, and supporting claims with reasons, evidence, and responding to diverse perspectives and values.
Common Course Numbering Language: Find, analyze, interpret, and evaluate primary and secondary sources, incorporating them into written work using appropriate documentation format without plagiarism.

Common Course Numbering Language: Draft and revise writing for style, diction, and tone showing awareness of audience and social context, and the purpose of the specific writing task; engage in a revision process so that language use does not impede clarity or disrupt meaning.
Common Course Numbering Language: Identify key elements of major genres (including poetry, drama, fiction) in order to analyze and interpret texts.
Common Course Numbering Language: Define common literary terms and apply these to analysis of specific texts.

IVC Details: Employ organizational structures to create cohesion, unity, and coherence in support of a central claim generated through analysis, interpretation, and evaluation of sufficient and relevant data and evidence.
IVC Details: Support arguments with direct quotation, summary, and paraphrase of both primary and secondary sources with appropriate citation conventions
IVC Details: Understand intellectual property and the ownership of ideas in academic research and writing.
IVC Details: Recognize and implement specific strategies for revision including conceptual features, organization, and audience.
IVC Details: Demonstrate sophistication in editing skills, fluency in academic writing in English, conventions of manuscript preparation, and citation conventions.
IVC Details: Honors: Demonstrate, through a formal presentation, research abstract, and/or annotated bibliography, the ability to locate, assess, and synthesize varied critical perspectives.

Accurately record the wave refraction and resultant direction of longshore transport.
Identify and classify the coastal depositional and/or erosional geomorphic features.
Analyze the cause and effects of sea level fluctuations, and identify and classify emergent and/or submergent coastal geomorphic features.

rows.title: Introduction to Global Studies

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes

objectives: analyze the history of globalization, including the role information and communication technologies have played in globalization.
describe and analyze key developments and characteristics of economic, political, cultural and ecological dimensions of globalization.
connect and analyze current developments in globalization from contemporary news to different dimensions of globalization.

rows.title: Introduction to Women, Gender, and Sexuality Studies
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: This course will examine the ways in which identities, sexuality, genders, race, and sex have been socially constructed and how these constructions change across different historical trajectories.

objectives: Analyze historical, social, political, and psychological forces that have led to the construction of gender in American society.
Evaluate the genealogies of feminist theories and the ways in which these concepts have translated into social movements from both a historical and contemporary perspective.

Identify the intersection between gender and various categories of difference including but not limited to race, ethnicity, class, age, nationality, ability, and sexuality and the ways in which these overlapping categories of difference affect an individual's experience and opportunity in American society.
Analyze the role of cultural representations of masculinity and femininity in the social construction of gender and sexual identities.
Identify the ways in which social and political activism and resistance have transformed notions of gender and sexuality historically and in contemporary society.

rows.title: Introduction to LGBTQ+ Studies
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Demonstrate comprehension of the development of LGBTQ+ rights movements in relation to broader social contexts.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Define the primary theories of identity, sexual orientation, and gender identity, and locate examples of each in contemporary cultural objects such as literature, fine arts, film, and digital media.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Utilize the concept of intersectionality to illuminate patterns of discrimination at intersections of sexual orientation, gender identity, race, ethnicity, class, dis/ability, and other social locations.

objectives: Apply concepts and theories in LGBTQ+ Studies, queer theory, and trans studies to contemporary social issues and cultural movements.
Trace the development LGBTQ+ identity theories from the introduction of the term “homosexuality” in the early 20th Century to the non-binaristic identity categories proliferating today.
Explain the differences between essentialist, social constructionist, and performative/queer theories of identity.
Discuss major concepts, figures, and priorities in trans studies and advocacy.
Define intersectionality and explain its importance in effectively understanding and advocating against discrimination.

Explain the major rights struggles and gains for LGBTQ+ individuals, including: decriminalizing existence and sex acts, military equity, hate crime legislation, marriage equality, and contemporary battles for trans rights and inclusion, among others.
Examine 21st Century achievements in LGBTQ+ acceptance and inclusion; explain how mainstreaming and white middle-class privilege created imbalanced gains.
Analyze a wide array of LGBTQ+ authored texts (music, literature, historical documents, art, among others) for philosophical and historical significance.
Analyze how capitalism, commodification, and neoliberalism inform LGBTQ+ life, organizing, and advocacy.
Examine the specific ways in which new technologies such as social media are utilized by queer culture and sub-cultures for expression, communication, community, and advocacy.
Identify the advocacy, activist, and cultural achievements of major figures in LGBTQ+ history

rows.title: Observation and Assessment of Young Children
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Evaluate the characteristics, strengths, limitations, and applications of contemporary observation and assessment tools.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Complete systematic observations and assessments of children’s development and learning using a variety of data collection methods to inform classroom teaching, environment design, interactions, and curriculum.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Describe the ethical and professional responsibilities for educators in observing and assessing young children’s development and learning.

objectives: Describe the legal and ethical responsibilities of a teacher or observer of children, including confidentiality related to observation and assessment.
Create a comprehensive portfolio on an individual child utilizing a combination of observation and assessment techniques.
Identify and evaluate challenges, biases, and preconceptions about assessing children.
Compare and analyze position statements of key professional associations regarding assessment and documentation.
Identify and apply basic quantitative and qualitative observation and recording techniques.
Compare and analyze traditional and current assessment tools and methods.
Articulate the value of involving families and other professionals in the observation and assessment process for all children.
Use observation tools to identify patterns, trends, and individual differences in groups of children.
Use observation tools to identify a quality in play-based environment, curriculum, and care routines.
Demonstrate and apply fundamental concepts of basic child development, specifically the developmental domains, to interpretations of observations.
Demonstrate and apply concepts of developmental domains when dealing with difference, delays, and disorders.
Illustrate the use of observation and assessment to implement curriculum and environmental changes in support of both group and individual needs.

rows.title: Principles and Practices of Teaching Young Children
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Compare and contrast historical and current early childhood education settings, issues, and perspectives.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Explain how foundational knowledge of child development and learning theories inform environments, pedagogy, and interactions in early care and education settings.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Identify the roles, requirements, and responsibilities of early childhood teachers as professional educators.

objectives: Describe historical and current issues as well as global approaches for early care and education.
Differentiate between various types of settings in relation to the ages served, regulations, and teacher requirements.
Identify the roles and responsibilities of an early childhood educator for curriculum and teaching, family engagement, ethical practice, and professional interactions with others in the classroom.
Identify and compare the developmental stages and needs of children, birth through age eight.
Describe Developmentally Appropriate Practice.
Explain the role and value of play.
Compare and contrast principles of positive guidance and interactions.
Explain how theories of learning and development guide early childhood environment design, curriculum, and teaching strategies.
Explain the ongoing curriculum cycle of observation, planning, implementation, and assessment.
Identify supports for first and dual language learners in developing English language and literacy skills including support for the home language.
Develop an initial personal philosophy of early childhood teaching

rows.title: Child Guidance and Discipline
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: SLO1 Identify and apply effective techniques for guiding children in the areas of personal care routines, outdoor play, creative art, sensory motor activities, science, math, and language and literacy.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: SLO2 Demonstrate the ability to use a series of positive guidance techniques.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: SLO3 Analyze the role of values and ethics in selecting and using developmentally appropriate positive guidance techniques which are respectful of the diversity of children and families.

objectives: Analyze and apply basic principles of child guidance and discipline.
Examine the theories of Piaget, Erikson, and Vygotsky and distinguish the role of each in applying positive guidance techniques.
Analyze the benefits of a strengths based approach to guidance.
Explain the multiple factors that make each guidance situation unique and apply that information in practical real life situations with children.
Articulate a professional philosophy of positive guidance based on basic principles of guidance and of basic child development, and incorporate differences in family and cultural background.
Apply effective communication techniques based on approaches of Ginott and Gordon and articulated by Faber and Mazlish in actual situations with children and adults.
Analyze and apply effective techniques for guiding children in all curricular areas.
Analyze the moral and ethical considerations in guidance techniques used with young children.
Analyze objective, written descriptions of children at play noting social interactions among adults and children.
Examine the effectiveness of strategies for guidance.

rows.title: Language and Literacy Foundations
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Describe techniques to foster emerging language and literacy in young children.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Evaluate language arts activities for their contribution to the phonological, phonemic and print awareness of the young child.

objectives: Evaluate language arts activities for their contribution to the phonological, phonemic and print awareness of the young child.
Compare and contrast the role of the school and the family in promoting literacy.
Assemble a collection of books, flannel board activities, poems, music, and other media to encourage literacy skills in young children.
Compare and contrast current national policies initiatives and historical views as they relate to early literacy.
Apply theoretical concepts and academic information from the course directly to effective planning of language and literacy activities.
Explain the variations in language acquisition rate due to factors such as gender, socioeconomic level, cultural context, and the health of the child.
Design a language and literature environment in the early learning classroom.
Evaluate and assess young children's literacy development.
Adapt instruction for children with special needs.
Integrate literacy activities throughout the curriculum.

rows.title: Health, Safety and Nutrition of Children
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Describe strategies used to promote the health, safety, and nutrition of children and adults in care and education settings.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Evaluate environments for both positive and negative impacts on children’s and adults’ health and safety.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Identify regulations, standards, policies, and procedures related to health, safety, and nutrition in care and education settings.

objectives: Define the broad concepts and practices of health, safety, and nutrition.
Identify laws and regulations related to health, safety, and nutrition.
Identify health and safety risks and prevention strategies in care and education settings.
Describe a caregiver’s role and responsibility in modeling good health, safety, and nutrition habits.
Describe culturally responsive strategies for partnering with families and the community in support of a healthy and safe environment for children.
Explore community resources available to support children and families
Apply the recommendations for children’s nutrition to the development of healthy and economical meals and snacks based on the age and individual needs of children.
Plan developmentally appropriate, culturally responsive learning experiences and environments that support the topics of health, safety, and nutrition.

rows.title: Practicum: Early Childhood Programs
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Design and implement curriculum and environments that are developmentally and linguistically-appropriate, engaging, and supportive of development and learning based on foundations of early childhood education and knowledge of individual children.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Apply a variety of teaching strategies, manage the classroom, monitor children’s development and learning, guide behavior, and use reflection on teaching practice to guide future planning.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Demonstrate the skills of a professional teacher including effective communication, ethical practice, responsibilities to children and families, and commitment to ongoing professional development.

objectives: Demonstrate developmentally, culturally, and linguistically appropriate practices as an early childhood teacher.
Analyze the ways in which individual values influence teaching methods and styles. Relate how your personal values influence your decisions as an early childhood professional. *
Apply the cycle of observation, planning, implementation, evaluation, and documentation in planning and implementing a developmentally appropriate curriculum. *
Apply current research and curriculum models and major child development theories in planning and implementing an appropriate play-based curriculum. *
Model and facilitate appropriate social interaction with adults and children with an emphasis on problem solving and conflict resolution.
Analyze the effect of the physical environment on the behavior and interactions of children and adults in the classroom and the outdoor play area. *
Analyze the role of indirect and direct techniques in guiding children and apply those techniques directly in the classroom*.
Critically assess personal classroom experiences and use information to develop more effective teaching and collaborative practices.
Develop a record-keeping system to document and track children's progress.
Demonstrate a professional level of competence in written and verbal expression.
Examine the implications of diverse family backgrounds in communicating effectively with parents and apply foundational theories in a classroom environment*.
Analyze coursework from throughout the early childhood program and be able to select examples supporting skills and information acquired, and experiences validated for professional portfolio. *
Evaluate personal progress and develop effective plans for on-going professional growth. *
Articulate and apply basic principles of effective advocacy.
*Meets critical thinking requirement.

rows.title: Teaching in a Diverse Society
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Examine the impact of various societal influences on the development of children’s personal and social identity.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Describe the ways that developmentally appropriate, inclusive, and anti-bias approaches support learning and development.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Identify the influence of teachers’ own culture and life experiences on teaching approaches and interactions with children and families.

objectives: Describe the nature and processes of systemic and internalized privilege and oppression and their impacts on children s identity development and learning.
Identify and assess the overt and covert ways in which stereotypes and prejudice are learned.
Analyze the unique and overlapping issues in racism, sexism, classism, heterosexism, ableism, and ethnocentrism as they relate to children and to early childhood settings.
Define issues of cultural identity including factors such as language, ethnicity, religion, immigration, and economic class, and relate these to children, families, and early childhood settings.

Define and assess the impacts of factors such as language, ethnicity, religion, immigration, and economic class in the personal history of the student and the subsequent impact on teaching young children and families.
Plan classroom environments, materials and approaches to effectively promote pride in one s own identity and delight and respect for social diversity.
Demonstrate strategies for helping children negotiate and resolve conflicts caused by cultural, class and gender differences, with a focus on using anti-bias approaches in the classroom.
Evaluate inclusive classroom environments, materials and approaches that are developmentally, culturally and linguistically appropriate to specific groups of children.
Describe a variety of strategies for creating partnerships with parents through building mutual, collaborative relationships, and to challenge bias and injustice in the lives of their children.
Evaluate professional ethics and responsibilities and legal implications of bias, prejudice and/or exclusion.

rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of how cultural and family contexts influence development. Students will score 70% or higher on a 5 point scale -multiple- choice exam.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Compare the developmental transitions involved in preparing children for school readiness and change from birth through adolescence. Students will score 70% or higher on a 5 point scale -multiple- choice exam.

objectives: Recognize and apply principal theories of development, research methods, historical perspectives on child development, ethical issues, and recent trends in the field.
Explain human development from conception through adolescence with emphasis on physical, cognitive, and psychosocial development within cultural and family contexts.
Compare major elements of language development throughout childhood.
Analyze and evaluate research methods and conclusions affecting our understanding of development.
Compare the developmental transitions involved in preparing children for school readiness and change from birth through adolescence.
Describe physical, cognitive and psychosocial developmental norms and deviations from typical development.
Demonstrate knowledge of how cultural and family contexts influence development.
Compare and contrast the historical perspectives regarding theory, research, and practices related to child development.
Apply theoretical concepts and academic information from the course directly to real life situations.

rows.title: Western Civilization: Beginnings to the Reformation
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Students will analyze a particular change in political, social, and/or economic organization in the western world (to 1500 C.E.) and explain its historical significance.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Students will explain the historical significance of a major discovery, invention, or scientific achievement in the western world (to 1500 C.E.).

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Students will explain the historical significance of a particular expression/movement in the art, architecture, and/or literature of the western world (to 1500 C.E.).

objectives: Interpret primary and secondary sources and to compose an argument that uses them, as appropriate,for support.
Explain and analyze the concept of "the West."
Explain and analyze changes in political, social, and economic organization in the western world and explain their historical significance.
Explain and analyze the historical significance of major philosophical, technological, and scientific developments.
Explain and analyze the historical significance in art, architecture, and literature.
Describe Hammurabi's rise to power and explain how his empire was governed.
List the key factors that shaped the earliest Mesopotamian cities.
Explain the nature and workings of transnational networks in the late Bronze Age.
Explain the rise of monotheism.
Describe and explain the factors that led to the rise of the Greek polis.
Define hoplite warfare and explain its effects on the development of democracy.
Explain the impact of the Persian and Peloponnesian Wars.
Describe Alexander's methods of conquest, colonization, and governance.
Describe the main characteristics of the Hellenistic world.
Explain the formation of the Roman Republic.
Explain the historical factors that shaped early Christianity.
Explain the differences (and similarities) between traditional Roman and Christian world views.
Describe the key features of Byzantine culture.
Explain the reasons for Islam's rapid expansion.
Explain the importance of the Carolingian Empire.
Explain the reasons for the fragmentation of power throughout most of Europe in the ninth and tenth centuries.
Explain the motivations for the Crusades and describe their main consequences.
Describe and explain the formation of papal power in Europe.
Explain the economic and social effects of the Black Death.
Describe and explain the causes, course, and consequences of exploration and colonization in the fourteenth through sixteenth centuries.
Explain the causes and consequences of the Reformation.
Identify and explain the medieval and early modern roots of the modern nation state.

rows.title: The History of World Civilizations to 1500 Honors
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Given a particular historical setting from early times to 1500 C.E., students will analyze the ways in which human groups have interacted with one another, including trade, migration, warfare, cultural exchange, and biological exchange.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Students will compare at least two distinctive forms of political, social, and economic organization in the world from early times to 1500 C.E. and explain their historical significance.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Students will explain the historical significance of a cultural development in art, music, architecture, literature or religion.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Students will identify a major discovery, invention, and/or scientific achievement (to 1500 C.E.) and explain its historical significance.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Students will identify and explain an example of a way in which the world's physical and natural environment has affected and been affected by developments in human history.

objectives: Relate and explain the arguments in favor of the African origins of humanity.
Describe the main features of Ice-Age civilizations.
Describe, compare, and explain the differences in paleolithic and neolithic cultures.
Explain how the environment affected the development of civilization in Egypt, Mesopotamia, the Indus River Valley, and in China.
Compare and explain the political, economic, and religious structures of early civilizations in Egypt, Mesopotamia, the Indus River Valley, and China.
Explain the basis for the success and (eventual) failure of the Hittite, Minoan, and Mycenaean states.
Explain why the Chinese and Egyptian civilizations were able to survive while other civilizations collapsed around 1000 BCE.
Describe the main features of Archaic Greek civilization.
List the most important developments during the Zhou dynasty in China and compare those developments with concurrent changes in the Ganges valley and in Sri Lanka.
Explain why the developments of civilization in the Americas and sub-Saharan Africa differed so dramatically from developments in Eurasia during the first millennium BCE.
Identify the key figures of the axial age and describe and explain key developments in axial-age political and religious thinking.
Explain the connections between the development of long overseas and overland trade routes and the rise of large empires across Eurasia in the first millennium BCE.
Describe and compare the great empires of Persia, Rome, Asoka, China, and Mesoamerica.
Describe and explain the rise of the Islamic Empire.
Describe and compare the Han, Sui, and Tang dynasties.
Describe and explain how and why Buddhism, Christianity, and Islam became world religions.
Explain the role of geography in the transmission of culture and development of states in sub-Saharan Africa and the Americas.
Describe how trading networks of the Indian Ocean affected the development of Ethiopia, India, and Southeast Asia 1000-1200 CE.
Describe the character, motivations, and affects of the Crusading movement.
Describe and compare how the Islamic Empire, the Byzantine Empire, and the Tang and Song Dynasties responded to invasions from peripheral peoples.
Describe the key features of Mongol civilization and explain why they were able to conquer their vast empire.
Describe and explain the effects of climate change, famine, and the plague on Eurasia during the fourteenth century.
Describe the key characteristics of the empires that developed in sub-Saharan Africa during the fourteenth to fifteenth centuries.
Describe and compare the key characteristics of the Aztec and Inca empires.
Explain the reasons for and consequences of the voyages of Zheng He.
Explain how and why Europeans began to explore new routes in the Atlantic during the fifteenth century.

Identify appropriate primary sources, analyze, evaluate, and interpret those sources, and deploy those sources in the development of an argument addressing some feature of civilization, daily life, culture, or social structure up to 1500 CE.

rows.title: America After the Bomb: 1945 to the Present
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Document Analysis/Critical Thinking/Historical Interpretation Given a particular historical setting from the Civil Rights period students will analyze primary documents from which historical analysis and critical historical interpretation will be given.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Using a primary source document from the Cold War era students will derive a thesis statement from a set of given evidence.

objectives: Describe the major elements of the dominant political, social, and economic issues of the post-war 1945 era as examined in this course.
Identify and describe the impact of the "containment" policy on post-war American society and its influence in shaping the politcal culture of post-war America.
Distinguish between historical analysis and factual narrative using primary and secondary document.
State and support a precisely worded thesis using primary and secondary sources from the cold-war era.
Recognize and criticize a historical argument in both primary and secondary materials.

rows.title: History of Ethnicity and Culture in the United States
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Given a particular primary source document, students will be able to articulate the differences between race as a social construction and ethnicity as a social construction.

objectives: Consider major patterns and factors that affect racial and ethnic identity and relations in the United States from the period of colonial American settlement to the present.
Assess the theoretical perspectives and paradigm shifts that are used to analyze racial and ethnic experiences in U.S. history.
Examine major historiographical debates surrounding the way in which race and ethnicity determine historical experiences.

Analyze the intersections between race and ethnicity and gender identity, class, age, citizenship status, sexual orientation, or other categories of marginalization in eras throughout United States history.
Evaluate the ways in which geographical location plays a role in shaping public and private discourse on race and ethnicity.
Compare patterns of development of racial and ethnic relations, inequality, and conflict in the United States and evaluate the ways in which these patterns are progressive or regressive.

rows.title: The History of East Asia Since 1800
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Critical Thinking/Historical Interpretation Students will analyze a particular change in political, social, and/or economic organization in the East Asian world (18th-21st century CE) and explain its historical significance.

objectives: Describe and critically evaluate the impact of Western scientific and political ideas during the late nineteenth century.
Identify and critically analyze the challenges to Chinese, Korean, and Japanese society from Western Europe and the United States.
Explain and evaluate the social and economic relations between the emerging scientific developments in Japan, Korea, and China and the emerging economic system of Industrialization.
Evaluate the social consequences of Westernization on Japanese society in the nineteenth century.
Distinguish between historical analysis using primary source documents and historical interpretation using secondary sources documents.
Formulate and support thesis using primary source documents on modern East Asian history.
Engage in textual analysis, evaluation, critique, and interpretation of themes and issues associated with historical questions and methodology appropriate to the study of Modern East Asian history.

rows.title: Women in American History Honors
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: By analyzing a prompt for a literary text, government document, or firsthand historical account, students will evaluate the way in which race and gender have intersected to create an increased burden on the lives of women of color in United States history.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Given a primary source report of a woman's experiences of inequality, students will provide an analysis of that experience based on the theoretical work of at least one prominent historian of U.S. women's history.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Presented with a primary source document from an early female settler to the American colonies, students will analyze and explain the way in which gender has shaped her perspective, experience, and opportunity in her "new world" setting.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Students will explain, analyze, and evaluate a prominent scholar's perspective on the role of feminism in advancing the status of women in the United States.

objectives: Debate the ways gender and sex can serve as analytical frameworks for historical inquiry.

Consider the ways in which women's history forces a divergent periodization of United States history and highlights various themes neglected when gender is not analyzed including women's life cycles, familial roles, domesticity, women's health issues, pregnancy and childrearing, and divisions of labor.

Distinguish the elements of transition from one historical era to another (e.g., from colonial conceptions of gender to Early Republican gendered roles or between the Era of the the "New Women" to the gender conformity of the post World War II period).
Assess the primary frameworks in which gender has been used as a category of historical analysis and evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of each methodology.

Identify and analyze the significance of the events and individuals (i.e., the Seneca Falls Conference, Elizabeth Cady Stanton, etc.) important to the course of women's history from the pre-contact period to the present.

Evaluate the intersection of gender and race, ethnicity, class, sexual orientaion, cisgender or transgender identity, or other categories of marginalization or privilege in society as such intersections relate to everyday life and large scale economic, political, intellectual, and social movements.
Distinguish, for each time period covered in scope of this course, the public and private experiences of women of different socio- economic status and geographic origin.

Evaluate the process of historical continuity and discuss the connection between our historical past and the present (e.g., Colonial antifeminism and current disparity between the earning power of me and women - the "glass ceiling").
Honors students will weigh the major arguments of prominent historians of women's and gender history and understand current scholarly debates surrounding major issues in the discipline.
Honors students will construct an original thesis and support the argument by conducting research outside of class.
Honors students will measure one's own original research in the context of major contemporary historiographical debates.

rows.title: Introduction to Environmental History

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Gain an understanding of the dynamic and complex place of the environment in world history, of interdisciplinary approaches to historical thinking, and of the ways in which their own lives are embedded in that history.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Learn to situate local experience, perception, and causes of environmental change within a global context. In other words, be able to identify the global forces at play in local concerns, but also the role that local action has in constituting global environmental systems.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Appreciate the ethical, cross-cultural, and historical context of environmental issues and the links between human and natural systems.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Learn how global historical processes like industrialization, urbanization, and the agricultural revolution have affected local environments.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Learn to apply particular environmental historical concepts to both historical and contemporary environmental issues. Concepts include environmental determinism/agency, urban metabolism, social construction of nature, social ecology, environmental justice, geographies of risk, and many others.

groups.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Gain a historical understanding of the Environment's relationship with the human condition (i.e. the Environment's philosophical, historical, literary, aesthetic, and cultural significance).

objectives: Describe the field of environmental history.
Discuss significant themes in environmental history.
Explain how historical events have been influenced by the natural environment.
Explain how human activity has altered the natural environment over time.

objectives: Common Course Numbering Language:
At the conclusion of this course, the student should be able to:
Demonstrate the ability to interpret primary and secondary sources and to compose an argument which uses supportive evidence.
Demonstrate an understanding of U.S. History through analytical categories such as race, class, gender, sexuality, ethnicity.
Analyze economic, political, and cultural developments as well as social movements and assess their historical significance.
Analyze the relevance of Modern American History to the present day.
IVC Details:

Identify the prevalent value system in a given period of American history and describe and discuss the nature in which those values are reflected artistic and architectural forms, the body of literature, the political institutions and legal mechanisms, the economic organizations, and the philosophic assumptions common in that period (e.g., American political theory and the Constitution, liberalism and the Progressive movement, the Puritan mentality and the novels of Horatio Alger; late 19th century feminism, and the NAWSA manifesto; the concept of the right of dissent and the poetry of Ginzburg or the essays of Martin Luther King etc.).

Describe the major elements of the dominant political, social, and economic structures, the religious ethos, and the intellectual and cultural achievements within any given period of American history from Reconstruction to the present.

Analyze the connection between individual function and contribution (e.g. labor roles) to a society and the method by which the society allocates social benefit, economic advantage, and political prerogrative.

Identify the elements of transition from one period to another (e.g., from the isolationist Gilded Age to the expansionist imperialist surge of the late 19th and early 20th centuries; from conformism of the 50's to the radical dissent of the 60's; etc.).
Identify fundamental elements of historiography and historical methodology.
Use basic reference works to locate more specific bibliographic and research material (from bibliographies and textbooks to monographs and articles.) This is an exercise in research method.
Distinguish between historical analysis and factual narrative.
Formulate a specific and focused thesis statement from a general historical premise.

Identify the central underlying themes in American history since Reconstruction and discuss the nature in which they interact (e.g., the economic context of post Civil War industrialization and the development of the Constitution in that period;, American frontier agrarian patterns and the spread of democracy in the early 19th century).

Explain the process of historical continuity and discuss the connection between the historical past and the present (e.g. the failure of "social reconstruction" as reflected in the abandonment of the former slaves after the Civil War and the persistance of racial tensions into the present).
